betterCitation: Francis Bacon, The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Of Death, the opening sentence (1625, modernised spelling)
reason: Broken on the edition, not the author. The card names only (1625), and the 1625 text does not read this way: the original-spelling text (Alfred S. West's Cambridge edition of 1908, on Wikisource as Bacon's Essays/Of Death) prints “Men feare Death, as Children feare to goe in the darke: And as that Natural Feare in Children is increased with Tales, so is the other.” The exact wording on the card, including the comma after “children”, exists only in the unattributed modernisation the verifier read (Gutenberg 575, whose sentence I downloaded and matched). The named modern editions differ from it: Mary Augusta Scott (1908) has “Men fear Death … natural fear in children is increased with tales” and the Harvard Classics (1909) has “Men fear death … natural fear in children is increased with tales”, both without that comma. So as printed the card attributes to 1625 a wording 1625 does not have. The house already settled this for Bacon: the May card reads Of Studies (1625, modernised spelling) with a note saying the modernised text is what was read, and the Of Adversity card names Scott’s edition. Fix either way: (a) keep the Gutenberg wording and use the corrected source line given here (114 characters, no dash, leads with the name), with a note that the wording is a modernised-spelling text of the 1625 Essays and that the quarto prints it in the spelling of its day; or (b) drop the comma after “children” and cite Scott, e.g. Francis Bacon, Essays, II, Of Death, the opening sentence (ed. Mary Augusta Scott, 1908), keeping her capital in Death. Also noted: Of Death first appeared in the 1612 Essays, so 1625 is the date of the text used, not of first publication. Everything else holds: the attribution is Bacon’s own and famous (it opens the essay), it is not on the misattribution list, shipped.js shows it is not shipped and has no near match, Bacon is at 2 (months 5 and 7) so this is his third and last line, he is not banned and he appears only once in November. It is in scope and publishable: the sentence is about the fear of death rather than about dying, and the later friars’ torture image is not quoted. The Essay tag is right.
